speechtext: That is not the question. Is my hon. friend bringing this question before the House at the instance of Captain Townsend?
Does that make any difference to the department? If that is all the excuse the minister has for his conduct in this case, it is not very good.

I must first thank my hon. friend for having been kind enough to advise me that he was going to bring up this question. I must thank him also for having postponed it until I had time to look into the papers and review the facts which have been brought to the attention of the department. I was absent when the decision was rendered by the then acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries, my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue, but I concur entirely and strongly in the views which he expressed in favour of the decision. The facts are the following. We have a law on the statute-book providing for the issue of licenses for whaling at points not less than fifty miles apart. As
my hon. friend has referred to that point, I may perhaps be permitted to read the provision of the law-section 9 of chapter 45, the Fisheries Act, which says :
No one shall at any time engage in the manufacture from whales of oil or any other commercial product, and no vessel or boat shall be employed in the whale fishery, except under _ license from the minister.
The minister may issue licenses to manufacture oil or other commercial product from whales or to employ boats or vessels in whale fishery, hut no such license shall issue until the minister has approved of the site of the factory, which shall not be within fifty miles of any other whale factory.
My hon. friend seems to take exception to the position taken by the department to the effect that no whale factory should be established, not merely within fifty miles, but within one hundred miles of any other whale factory. I may tell my hon. friend immediately why we came to that decision. Our law is copied from that of Newfoundland, and I am sorry to find that the Newfoundland whale fisheries, which at one time were a very prosperous industry, are now dying out if they are not entirely dead, and the reason for that is that too large a number of whale fishing licenses were issued. After having discussed the question with the officers of the department who had made a special study of it, we decided that we should not issue any license for a whale factory less than one hundred miles from the site of another whale factory. I may say that all the licenses on the British Columbia coast were so advised during the discussion of the Bill that was before parliament in the session of 1904. Several applications had been received from British Columbia for licenses. These applications stood in abeyance until the Bill should become law, and the parties interested were so advised. After the Bill was passed, a copy of it was sent to each of them. No application was received for a certain time except from the Pacific Whaling Company. That company, if I remember rightly, started two factories on the west coast of Vancouver Island in 1905, and it was the only applicant for a license up to that time.
They got the whole west coast of the island.
They have only two licenses, which were issued for the western coast of Vancouver Island. No more than that number could be issued for that coast.
What is the length of the coast?

I do not remember exactly. The company got two licenses for the western coast of the island. I think one is at Parker's Sound and the other at Esperanzo Inlet. Mr. Townsend applied for a license at a place which was less than fifty miles from either of these places, and

of course under the law we could not grant him a license. I am stating these facts because I want to show to my hon. friend and to impress upon the House the kindness with which the department dealt with Mr. Townsend; and my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue put a very proper question when he asked my hon. friend (Mr. A. A. McLean) whether he was speaking on the advice of Captain Townsend or not; because I understand that Captain Townsend knows all the circumstances, and would not blame the department for the stand it has taken on this matter.
His letter which I read does not indicate that.
Yes, but will my hon. friend tell us where he got information or a letter from Captain Townsend complaining of the action of the government and asking him to bring this question before the House ?
I read the letter to the House addressed by Captain Townsend to the minister in which he complained of the treatment accorded him by the government in the matter.
After the decision -was rendered ?
Not exactly after, because there was really no decision then.

Before the decision was rendered. If my hon. friend had asked for the documents he would have found that we have treated Captain Townsend in the fairest way and that there was no intent, direct or indirect, to hurt him in any way. Going on with the facts I was relating, in the fall of 1906, some time after I entered the department, there were several applications still standing, and the Pacific Whaling Company asked for two or three more licenses. Before issuing those licenses I had a letter addressed to all applicants who had put in their applications some one, two or three years before, asking them whether they intended to proceed with their application, because I did not want, for my part, to give all the coast to one company, although this company was a Canadian company. I shall read that letter in order that the House may see the fairness with which these applicants, including Captain Townsend, were treated. The letter reads :
October 1, 1906.
Sir,-With reference to your application for whale factory licenses on the Pacific coast at -I may say that various and conflicting applications have been filed fotr such licenses, in the light of which, under the terms of the Act-1 Edward VII, chapter 13-copy inclosed, the minister is unable, owing to the tentative character of the several applications, to decide as to the issue of such licenses.
In order, therefore, that all -applications may be properly before the minister, and so entitled to consideration, it is essential that Mr. BRODEUR
within a month from the date of this letter, all those who have already applied at any time and under anv conditions, for such licenses, and who intend to follow up such applications must-
Now we give in this letter the requirements of the law:
1.	File the necessary assurance that the factory when completed will be capable of converting any whale captured into commercial products within 21 hours of the landing thereof, and thiat the business will be conducted in sucb a manner, etc., etc.
2.	Pile plans and specifications of the machinery to be used.
3.	Forward to this department the fee of $800.
I go further in this letter and draw the attention of those applicants to the fact that the intention of the department was to restrict the issuing of those licenses within 100 mile limits. Here is the part of the letter dealing with that part of the question :
Owing to the experience in the industry in Newfoundland waters, and in view of strong representations to the minister as to the probable decline of the new industry in Canadian waters, under similar conditions, he has decided that both on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts no further licenses for whale factories will be granted nearer to each other than 100 miles instead of 50 as contemplated by the Act.
I am, sir,
Your obedient servant,

Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I do not think my hon. friend will take exception to the position then taken by the department. It is of the utmost importance that our fishing' industry should be preserved in this country and the only way of preserving this industry is by issuing proper regulations in order to prevent the operation of the fisheries. The whale fishery was in the same position. I thought, and the advise of the officers of the department was to the same effect, that it was necessary that we should be more careful and cautious than they were in Newfoundland and prevent the industry from being absolutely destroyed.
Was the change from 50 miles to 100 miles made by order in council or by departmental regulation?

By regulation of the department, and it was of course binding upon all the applicants. It was intended simply not to have too many whale factories established in this country in order to preserve the fisheries, relying upon the experience in Newfoundland waters.
Is there any regulation which limits the catch ?

No. In the law there is a provision, however, that they must use only one boat, that is the only restriction in

that respect. It is not to be expected they could catch more than about one whale a day in good weather. I was saying to the House that later on, in December, 1906, the Pacific Whaling Company applied for more licenses and I thought that an opportunity should be given to the applicants who showed some desire to carry out their works to do so, and that we should show them that their applications for licenses would be carefully considered. I refused then to issue any licenses to the Pacific Whaling Company until I had ascertained what Captain Townsend was ready to do, and I gave him six months for that purpose. He made his application which was put in within the six months. I was away at the time but the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) was then acting as Minister of Marine and Fisheries. We got information that Captain Townsend was not acting for himself but was acting for a foreign company with foreign capital and foreign labour.
Will tjie minister state from whom he received that information ?
Yes, and I understand my hon. friend will not deny it, because I understand him to say that a man named Larsen, who was a foreigner I understand from Norway, was applying.
I did not state exactly that. I stated that Mr. Larsen represented a firm of London financiers and that he was a Norwegian and was putting money in it, only a portion of the total.

Will my hon. friend state here-because I consider it is important and he must be aware of it-that this company on behalf of which Captain Townsend applied for a license was not a company composed in the majority of foreign capital with foreign labour and foreign vessels ?
I do not think there is anything at all on the record or that the government has any information that foreign vessels were going to enter this industry.

I am asking my hon. friend whether he will give us this information. But I have some information here on the file. First, we have a telegram here from Captain Balcom in which he states :
Townsend as it is known as he stated to me himself is negotiating to sell out his license if he should get it, to a Norwegian concern.
I think that is some evidence.
The Norwegians as you know have the right to bring into Canada their vessels free of duty while I had to pay duty having my Norwegian built steamers brought into Canada under English flags and they can without being liable to prosecute bring in alien contract 326
labour signed on as crew of their vessels at rates of wages so far below current wages here as to demoralize rates of wages in the industry to the serious injury of all workmen engaged in it this will give foreigners a great advantage over our company and the ninety-four Canadian shareholders of our company feel indignant about such possibilities and hope that speculators like Townsend who simply will sell out Canadian resources to foreigners will not be given a preference over Canadians who have been the pioneers in this new industry on this coast, and have spent large amounts of money to prove that this industry can successfully be conducted on this coast and have spent large sums for acquiring the process which complies strictly with the Canadian Whaling Act and who have been the first applicants for Banks Island district, and who have made the complete application demanded by law.
Is it not a fact that Capt. Balcom sold his license to the Pacific Whaling Company ?

Yes-that Is the Canadian company; ninety per cent of its capital is British Columbia capital, while the majority of the capital of the other company is foreign capital, the vessels it was going to use were foreign vessels which would come here without being obliged to pay duty, and it would employ foreign labour which would seriously demoralize the labour market on the British Columbia coast. I have also to point out a communication from Messrs. Drury & Hall, two prominent citizens of British Columbia, who sent the following telegram to the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) :
We earnestly beg your utmost influence prevent license being granted Norwegian Company operating foreign bottoms whaling off British Columbia coast. This resource should be conserved for benefit of Canadians and Canada.
Besides that I would call attention to a letter we received from the attorneys, Messrs. Barnard & Robertson, to H. B. Mc-Giverin, of which perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. A. A. McLean) would not give us information. The letter is dated, Victoria, June 3, 1907, and says :
We have to advise you that our clients have entered into an agreement with Captain Townsend providing for the acquisition of the whaling license granted to him.
So, it would seem from this letter that those interested in the whaling license was not Capt. Townsend, but some clients of Messrs. Barnard & Robertson, that is the foreign company which my hon. friend has mentioned. I think there is not the least doubt that foreign capital, foreign labour, foreign vessels to be engaged in the whale fishing in this country is to the detriment of our own people, our own shipping and our own capital. The Minister of Inland Revenue, in view of the situation, decided- 1 and decided properly; I strongly support the



decision he has rendered-to protect our Canadian people rather than the foreigners. I am surprised that my hon. friend (Mr. A. A. McLean) comes here and attacks the department for having tried to protect Canadian labour against foreign labour, Canadian shipping against foreign shipping. Canadian capital against foreign capital. That is the position the department has taken, and I stand by it, I leave the case in the hands of the House, confident that the House will declare that the department has taken the course which should command the approval of the country.

The minister is very eloquent over the question of foreign labour and capital. He was not quite so strong on the foreign question when he was getting in the foreigner Falconer here to reorganize the accounts of his department. At that time, it was entirely immaterial, and the minister was qnite oblivious for a long time until the opposition enlightened him as to the conditions surrounding that transaction.
Now, what I gather from the transaction is this : It is not so much a question of the foreigner, as it is of giving a peculiar and very unjustifiable monopoly to the Pacific Whaling Company, who have, by some means, got the ear of the department of the government, to the extent even (so far as I can see) of repealing a statute which this parliament saw fit to pass. That is the extraordinary position that the Minister of Marine admits. We have a statute, section 9 of the Fisheries Act, which defines the terms upon which licenses shall be granted and defines the policy laid down by parliament as to the regulation of whale fishing. This section says what the minister shall do and what he shall not do. And, among other things, it provides that licenses shall be granted for the establishment of whaling factories at distances not less than fifty miles apart along the coast. That is as I understand it-I have not looked at the statute. Now, what does the minister purport to do? To repeal this statute which parliament made. Forsooth, because some person wants to come in between the 100-mile-distant stations of the Pacific Whaling Company, the minister promulgates a regulation-it is not even done by order in council,-which purports to repeal the statute which parliament had passed and says that licenses shall be granted to establish factories at distances of not less than 100 miles. This is a very extraordinary position to take. We have had many extraordinary developments under this administration, but none, I think, more extraordinary or more defiant of the law than this. I venture to say to the minister, with a great deal of confidence-notwithstanding that he is a very prominent and able lawyer-that, on consideration he will have to come to the Mr. BRODETTR.
conclusion that he has absolutely no power
to do anything of the kind, but that when parliament passes a statute defining the conditions upon which licenses shall be granted, then, upon those conditions and those only can licenses be granted. And when the minister sees fit to send a letter, for which he takes credit, to Capt. Townsend, not only saying that if they want a license they must follow up their application within a certain time

which may be all right, but when he gives the various parties notice that no licenses shall be granted to establish a factory within 100 miles of any other factory, he undertakes to say what was not in contemplation by parliament and he professes to lay down a law which is not the law of Canada. More than that, he does a very unfair thing, because he warns off these men-just as we had a case of warning off by another minister. I say he warns off these men by giving them to understand that they have no chance under the conditions he lays down. This is matter of very serious complaint not only by Capt. Townsend, but by this parliament. For, when we pass a law, no minister has a right to vary that law; only parliament can do that.
I have said, the minister was very eloquent on the question of foreign labour and foreign capital, and so on. I do not know whether I caught the name correctly, but the minister read to us a statement of Capt. Barker, or some such name, against Capt! Townsend, in which Capt. Townsend is characterized as a speculator and so on. The minister will get mountains of evidence of that kind if it suits his mind. You merely want the statement of the rival of a man running in the same race, and if the minister is prepared to decide upon that kind of evidence, he will get any amount of it at all times. But I submit that is no evidence at all. On the other hand, there is no evidence that Capt. Townsend was a speculator, or that he should not receive better treatment than the government gave him, and that his application should be ignored while at least three additional licenses were granted to the Pacific Whaling Company. The minister should have regarded his application in a more favourable light. In Canada we are seeking to induce foreigners, from Norway and Sweden, as well as other European countries, to come here and settle. Some of them bring in capital and others do not. Surely it should not be an obstacle to a man getting a license that his capital comes from Norway. The anxiety of the minister to exclude foreign capital from Canada, to prevent Norwegians coming to settle in Canada and adding to our wealth, is in direct contravention of the policy of his government in respect to immigration, and I think the administration deserves censure for their attitude in this matter.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lennox), if he has any evidence to show that the Norwegians who have engaged in the coasting trade of Canada have ever invested any capital in Canada?

I am not at all concerned about the abstract question, but I am concerned with the matter which has been brought before the House. There is evidence given by my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. McLean), that there was a bona fide application, not only to invest money, but to engage in an enterprise that would be profitable to Canada, and by a class of men who would be a distinct acquisition to the industrial life of Canada if they had been allowed to get the license.

Let me tell the hon. gentleman and the House, in addition to what I have already said, that the fishery regulations provide that the licenses shall only be given to British subjects. Of course we have to follow the same rule In this case.
Mr. Townsend was a British subject.
But he was acting for foreigners.

Only to the extent of $60,000. There is no evidence before the House that Norwegians were taking their vessels out to engage In this industry, nothing but the word of Captain Balcom who represents the Pacific Whaling Company.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. TEMPLEMAN (Minister of Inland Revenue).
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Having had something to do -with the issue of this license to the Pacific Whaling Company, I may say a few words on the question. Referring to the remarks of my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), he said that the minister had practically changed the law by fixing the distance between whaling factories one hundred miles instead of fifty. Section 9, clause 2, regarding whale fishing, reads :
The minister may issue licenses to manufacture oil or other commercial products from whales and to employ boats or vessels in whale fishery, but no such license shall issue until,-
(a) The minister has approved of the site of the factory, which shall not be within fifty miles of any other whale factory, or in such proximity to any inhabited place or places as in the opinion of the minister, may cause danger or detriment to the public health.
I am not a lawyer, but it seems to me that under the clause the minister may issue licenses at his own discretion, or he may, by order in council, or by regulation established by himself, determine that no two licenses shall come within one hundred miles of each other. The minister, according to the advice he received from his offi-3264
cers, and having in view the depletion of the whale fishery on the Atlantic coast, particularly around Newfoundland, decided that for the present, at all events, and until he knew how this industry was going to succeed in the Pacific ocean, decided not to place them closer on the Pacific coast than one hundred miles. I think therefore that the charge of the hon. member for Simcoe that the minister was violating the Act. is unfounded. The hon. gentleman also said that there was a monopoly given to the Pacific Whaling Company. This also is inaccurate, inasmuch as there have been two other whaling licenses granted. They are now in the hands of the parties to whom they were issued, one in March of this year to Mr. Georg*e H. Huff, of Alberni, on Vancouver Island ; and one in July, 1907, to Dr. Francis Walter Hall, at Rose Harbour, Queen Charlotte island. Here we have two licenses issued to parties other than the Pacific Whaling Company, which licenses by the way, have not yet been used, though one company I am advised has been formed. I presume it nfieans to secure the capital to build a factory. Now if our Norwegian friends who had so much capital to invest in this business, were very anxious to engage in the industry, why did they not form a company in alliance with Dr. Hall, of the city of Victoria, and utilize his license and start the industry ? They can do the same in respect of the whaling license given to Mr. Geo. A. Huff, on the southern "end of Queen Charlotte island, and start a whale industry if they so desire. These gentlemen are probably looking for capital and for experienced men who understand the catching and preparation of whales for commercial purposes.
Now some remarks were also made about the bona fides of the applicants. The application of Captain Townsend was bona fide. He is a well known citizen of Victoria, and captain of one of th'e Canadian Pacific Railway steamers on the west coast of Vancouver island. His application as made was bona fide. He could have organized a company to start the industry, just as Captain Balcom did before him. Captain Townsend had made sev"eral applications, but as they interfered with the others, he withdrew them. Finally he placed before the department an application for a license in the vicinity of Campania island off the north coast of the mainland and not far from the Queen Charlotte islands. The Pacific Whaling Company had, a year or six months before that, put in an application for a whaling license on Banks island, both islands being within thirty or forty miles of each other-probably less. Captain Balcom put in an application for a. license for Banks' island on October 20, 1906, and Captain Townsend put in his application for Campania island on June 3, 1907. Before six months elapsed Captain Townsend made his application good under the Act. He put

up $800 and lie gave assurances in writing to the minister that the machinery would be provided that would dispose of a whale in twenty-four hours.
He complied with the conditions of the Act ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
He complied with the conditions. Captain Balcom did the same thing in respect to his Bank island application. The whaling industry was started in British Columbia in 1904. Captain Balcom Is the pioneer of the industry. He was a sealing captain from Nova Scotia who had been engaged for many years in catching seals in Behring sea. When that industry began to go down he turned his attention to whaling. He investigated the possibilities of whaling. He travelled through the east, investigated the conditions in Newfounland, studied all he could about it, applied for the first license, got up a local company and secured capital in the city of Victoria. He invested $150,000 in his first whaling factory at Sechart immediately north of Barclay Sound on the west coast of Vancouver island. His first efforts very nearly resulted in failure. He struggled hard for nearly a year. He found that, with the mechanical and chemical process he had introduced, it was impossible to extract all the oil out of the whale and his venture was very nearly a failure. It was at that time that applications for licenses came in from a great many other people. Captain Townsend is not the only man who has failed to receive a license. There have been half a dozen others. The Pacific Whaling Company, after the first year's operations, very nearly became a failure because of their inability to manufacture the whale oil and fertilizer so that the products would be commercially profitable. They looked around and they found a gentleman named Rismuller, a German, who had a process of his own, the value of which was in the chemicals used as well as in the machinery. The Pacific Willing Company made a contract with Dr. Rismuller. I do not know whether a certain sum of money was paid or whether a large interest was given in the industry, but I know that it cost the Pacific Whaling Company a very large consideration to get Dr. Rismuller to go into the industry so that his process could be adopted. Dr. Rismuller went into it and the Pacific Whaling Company was a success from that time on. They have been making money since. Now, this is the position :	Captain Sprott Balcom was the
pioneer of the industry. Ninety per cent of the capital invested in the Pacific Whaling Company is owned by Victoria people. Captain Balcom, in his first efforts, bought a sealing steamer in Norway. A sealing steamer is not an ordinary steamer. It is constructed in such a way as to be adapted to the modern requirements for Mr. TEMPLEMAN
catching whales. He changed the flag and brought the steamer into Victoria. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) insisted on his paying the duty on it although Captain Balcom thought that as it was a new industry he should be relieved of the duty. But, the Minister of Customs would not relent and this company *when it was struggling against many diflicultes, had to pay to the government about $7,000 upon that steamer. That was the position when my attention was called to the matter in the department. Let me say that Captain Townsend is not a party to this discussion. Barnard & Robertson, as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) knows, is a good Conservative firm in Victoria. Mr. Barnard is president of the Conservative Association of British Columbia and he very probably sent down here some letters, all of which are on file, to the leader of the opposition who has passed them on to the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I., (Mr. Mc.Lean) and that hon. gentleman has thought to make a charge against this government of partiality in awarding this license to the Pacific Whaling Company as against Captain Townsend. I said, in a letter to Captain Townsend, that I would investigate the facts on the ground. When I went to British Columbia last fall I learned that Captain Townsend had little or no capital of his own. Very probably he had some friends who' might have subscribed if he had organized the company. I found that there were Norwegian gentlemen on the ground waiting to get that license. Very probably they would have organized a company if they got it. I am not saying anything against Captain Townsend associating himself with Norwegian capitalists or whaling men; he had a right to do so. But that company could have brought a Norwegian steamer into British Columbia to engage in the whaling industry without paying any duty on her. At that time it was possible to do so under the Act, but since then the Act has been changed and it is not possible now.
Is there anything in the papers to substantiate that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No. I learned this on the ground. It was pointed out by Captain Balcom, managing director of the Pacific Whaling Company. That was the danger. It could have been done and Captain Balcom had paid $7,000 duty on his steamer. Captain Balcom had at that time under way his second station under the three first licenses and had purchased a second steamer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Certainly; he is the managing director of the Pacific Whaling Company. I do not know how Mr. Bnlcom transferred his license to the company, but I know he organized the company and secured the capital. There are over eighty residents of Victoria who are stockholders in the Pacific Whaling Company, of which Captain Balcom is the managing director, and D. Rismuller is the practical man in charge of the practical work at the factories. They have made a great success of the enterprise. The Pacific Whaling Company is absolutely a Canadian undertaking. Captain Townsend proposed to organize a Norwegian Company, and for myself I do not care whether the capital was to come from Norway or not, but there was the danger that they would bring their vessel in without paying duty and that she would be manned by Norwegians. I may say that the expert high-priced harpooners in the Pacific Whaling Company to-day are Norwegians. Captain Balcom, representing the Pacific Whaling Company, applied for Banks island before Captain Townsend applied for the island contiguous to it. The Pacific Whaling Company had made good the year before. We knew that their plant was satisfactory and we knew they had been successful in business and that they had the capital to carry it on. Putting all these things together and after having several interviews with Captain Townsend, I decided that the license should go to the Pacific Whaling Company for Banks island, which being within ioo miles of the island for which Captain Townsend had applied, necessarily under the rule precluded the application of Captain Townsend being granted. X want to say to the House and to my hon. friend (Mr. McLean) who has been primed for this occasion, not by Captain Townsend, but by Barnard and Robertson, a legal firm of Victoria, I want to say that if Captain Townsend was their client, they are acting contrary to his wishes.
Do you know that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: What ?
Do you know that your statement is a fact, or is it only surmise ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I repeat that the hon. member is not acting under instructions from Captain Townsend.
How do you know that?
The minister stated that this law firm was acting contrary to the instructions of their client. Does he know that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I say they are not acting under instructions from Captain Townsend, who although not a consenting party to the final disposal of this license, saw the reasonableness and fairness of it. Knowing Captain Townsend as I do, I am safe in saying that my hon. friend (Mr. McLean) in bringing this matter before the House was not acting upon the suggestion of Captain Townsend, who was the principal in the whole transaction.
Mr. I'OSTEIt. That is only a supposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Quite true, it is only a supposition, but it is a natural one. It was on my instructions the deputy nj blister gave the license to the Pacific Whaling Company, and I wrote him from Victoria the following letter :
Victoria, British Columbia,
September 6, 1907. Lieutenant Colonel Gourdeau,
Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Colonel,-I to-day wired you as follows : ' In the matter of whaling license issue to the Pacific Steam Whaling Company at Banks island, if they have complied with conditions/
I have examined into the case, and I believe on every ground that will be the best thing to do. It will be best in the public interest generally. This company is a purely Canadian enterprise while the rival applicant would be foreign when constituted. The Pacific Company also has demonstrated by successful operation of other stations that it is possessed of the practical knowledge necessary to carry on the business, while its machinery and system of working is superior to that of any other company.
Under this decision to grant a license to the Pacific Company the application of Captain Townsend cannot be granted. His deposit should, therefore, be returned to him and he should be informed that the application of the Pacific Company has been favoured for the reasons above stated, and especially because the plant and machinery of the Pacifio Company meets the requirements of the department while those of Captain Townsend do not.
The last words ' while those of Captain Townsend do not ' might possibly have been omitted, inasmuch as Captain Townsend had no plant or machinery, although he stated to the department that he would provide such plant and machinery as would meet with the approval of the department. I believe I gave this decision in the best interest of all concerned. I repeat that Captain Townsend did not express himself as dissatisfied when the decision was arrived at and therefore there can be_ no grievance, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. McLean) cannot find any condemnation of the department on the action taken.
How many licenses has the Pacific Whaling Company ? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Five.
Covering what extent of coast line ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They are obliged to be 100 miles apart. They have three factories now running and they contemplate a fourth. They have the license at Banks island in the north and one on Fitzhugh sound. As I have mentioned there are two other licenses issued and not utilized to-day. I understand that there are others who are making applications for licenses. There is an application for the Queen Charlotte islands. There is one license granted at the south end of Queen Charlotte islands and there is an application for one at the north end.
Is the whole coast line taken up ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not think the coast line of British Columbia is taken up yet. For these licenses they have to pay $800 for the first year. $1,000 for the second year, and $1,200 for the third year, and this being the second year for Banks island license, this company is paying $1,000 for that license whether they use it or not. If the licenses are not utilized within a given time the minister has power to cancel them so that the public interest is well protected.
I cannot make out from what the minister has said as to whether the number of licenses granted now really pre-empts the whole coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I said that it certainly did not take up the whole coast.

It must come pretty close to it. You have five of them, besides two granted which are not in use, all belonging to the Pacific Company, I understand. That makes seven licenses, which would take up 700 miles.
There are the Queen Charlotte islands and the eastern coast of the Island of Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I might inform my hon. friend that seven licenses might be placed around the island of Vancouver alone, as it is 300 miles long.
Is the limit that they shall not be within 100 miles of each other, or is the coast line measured?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think the measurement is by water.
What I wanted to ask the minister was this. Does he argue for a monopoly because the Pacific Whaling Company is a Canadian company and has put in its money?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not argue auv-thing of the kind. If the application of the Pacific Whaling Company for Banks island 1
Mr. FOSTER,
had not been in months before the other, and if they had not complied with all the conditions equally with Captain Townsend, if they had not made good under the law, there is no question that the license would have gone to Captain Townsend, which shows that I had no desire to create any monopoly.
Why did you say to Captain Townsend that you were going to give him a license and afterwards rescind that by reason of the fact that he was engaging foreign capital?
It was simply because information had reached the department that it was foreign capital after the date of the letter of October, 1906.
Is it intended to discourage the introduction of foreign capital ?

No, but the great disadvantage in this case was this. The vessels it was proposed to use in the business were vessels to be brought from Norway, and we are obliged to admit free of duty Norwegian vessels which come here to engage in the coasting trade.

I did not intend to speak in this debate, but I would not think it wise to adopt a policy which would discourage the introduction into this country of capital from abroad, because if there is one thing that Canada needs more than an: other it is the introduction of capital from abroad in any of our industrial activities.
But in this case there is a clause in our regulations providing that licenses shall be issued only to British subjects.

That may be a vpry proper provision, but I understand that Captain Townsend is a British subject; and so far as shipping is concerned, any objection on that score must be an objection to the customs law, and not a special objection to the project that was on foot at the instance of Captain Townsend. However, the matter has been debated, and I do not desire to delay the House "with any consideration of that. I rose merely for the purpose of uttering a protest against the obvious attempt of the Alinister of Inland Revenue to cast some slur or discredit upon Alessrs. Barnard and Robertson. Eventually he stated that the matter to which he alluded was a conjecture or surmise in his own mind more than a matter of positive knowledge, as far as these gentlemen are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I drew an inference, as you do.

I do not think I am in the habit of drawing inferences to the discredit of any gentleman who is not

In this House to defend himself. If I have ever done so, I have done it inadvertently.
I do not think the hon. gentleman can point to any instance; if he can, let him do It now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: What discredit ?
If the hon. gentleman's remarks meant anything, they meant that for political purposes these gentlemen were disregarding their duty to their client.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I said that Captain Townsend was their client and not the Norwegian representative. I said they were acting contrary to the wishes of their client, because I knew the wishes of Captain Townsend in this matter.

The wishes of Captain Townsend or the wishes of the Norwegian representative or any one else did not make the slightest difference. This was a matter touching the policy of the government, and such matters are not to be controlled according to the desire of Captain Townsend or this Norwegian gentleman or any one else. It is a matter of public in-1 terest, not a matter of private interest, that is being discussed on this occasion. That is a sufficient answer to what the hon. gentleman has alleged just now and during his speech. I think it is a matter of regret that a minister of the Crown should make a statement of that kind founded on mere conjecture. He covers it of course with an 'if'; he says if such and such was the case these gentlemen apparently were disregarding their duty to their client and using their position for political purposes. So far as I know these gentlemen, and I know something of them, they are men who stand well in their profession, and their reputation in the community in which they are known is fully equal to that of the Minister of Inland Revenue, and it does not become him as a minister of the Crown to endeavour to cast any such aspersion upon them as he endeavoured to do this afternoon.
It might be said that the minister's statement was not an Inference; it was a presumption.

Mr. Speaker, before the motion carries, I would like to say that I understand that the militia estimates are to be considered in Supply. I had intended to discuss these estimates somewhat fully in the House, as to administration and as to policy; but at this hour I thought I would propose to the House, particularly to my hon. friends opposite, whether the real discussion might not be taken up at some future date, and the House go into committee now to pass if possible one or two urgent items. I would suggest, for instance, that the large vote on page 37. $1,300,000, which is not immediately required, might be allowed to stand over, and that upon that Item the whole question of the militia might be discussed at some
future time. As to the principal militia items, four of them are urgent-pay and allowances, that is, for the permanent force, which is at present without pay; annual drill, which to be of any use must be voted at once and voted in full, because most of the camps will come on in the next few weeks; salaries and wages, which are required monthly; and the Dominion arsenal.
I would like to call attention to the item of annual drill.
And transport?

The annual drill involves the transport.
Mr. FOSTER, Then really the urgent item is annual drill.
Yes.
How long will it take to tell about the annual drill?
My officers are here, we have 55 minutes and perhaps I could explain it in that time. If not it would be necessary that the item I mention on page 37 would be open to full discussion.
We could even discuss the annual drill upon that.

Certainly.
Motion agreed to and House went into Committee of Supply.
Militia-annual drill, $1,000,000.

The understanding is that we will take up item 74 about which the minister will make any such statement as seems to him necessary. So far as the more general statement to which he alluded is concerned, the proposal is that it shall be reserved until some future occasion on some item.

Yes. The amount spent upon the annual drill last year, ending March 31, was $1,085,000. It is not proposed to spend any more on annual drill this year than last year. We intend to make our arrangements in such a way as to keep within that limit.

Is the increase of $155,000 due to the same reason that was given the other evening by the Minister of Railwavs and Canals, namely that what were formerly supplementary estimates are now included in the main estimates ?
Yes.
Is it true that there is a good deal of money owing to some of the militia men for last year? I heard a complaint of that the other day.
No, there is not a dollar.
That is extraordinary. A militiaman told me that there was some owing from last year. I told him we had voted $200,000 this year on account of some balance that remained over from last year.
I am informed that every single corps has been paid up to the last cent.
I am glad to hear my hon. friend say so. I shall send the ' Hansard ' to the party concerned to-morrow.
How many troops do you propose to have at annual drill this year ?
The same number as last year. The total number is 45,000 and there will be about 30,000 in camp, the balance will be drilled at headquarters in tlie cities.
That is the full strength?
Yes.
Will you count the trip of those who go to the tercentenary as equivalent to the annual drill ?

Yes that will be so with the rural militia. The city corps will receive their full 12 days' pay which they will use as they choose but thev will not be paid for the four days at Quebec. Of course all their transportation and subsistence will be paid, but the actual time at Quebec will not be paid. They will be given the money for the 12 days' drill. They will drill locally and will go to Quebec free of any further charge except their transportation and subsistence.
How about the rural militia ?

It is intended to take one company from each rural regiment. That company will not go to camp but will go to Quebec and will be paid for going to Quebec the number of days that the trip occupies, probably it will be the full 12 days but it will not exceed that.

I do not think I agree with that idea. It seems to me that you should have the annual drill before the ter-centary and then make your selection. I suppose the idea of making the selection is to have the very best company, and the best way to find out which is the best company is by observation during the annual drill. You have no other way of testing themi as I understand, in the rural regiments because the company that perhaps made the best showing last year would not make the best showing this year owing to the numerous changes that take place, particularly in infantry regiments, from year to year.
In many cases the drill will take place first, but the
matter of selection will be left entirely to the regiments.
But you say the men who go to Quebec will not go to camp.

My hon. friend should not tie me up too close. What will happen will be this : Suppose a regiment is 350 strong, and that we intend to send, and I believe it is intended to send, a company of the strength of 45 to Quebec. In that particular regiment the commanding officer will be instructed that he can only take 305 men to camp but we shall not tell him that he may not take to Quebec some of those who go to camp. We cannot afford to pay any more, otherwise we would not be able to send these men to Quebec at all without an extra vote.

Then I think you had better take the extra vote. That does not seem to me to be the right way to do this thing. Drill the different regiments and then select the very best company from each regiment to take to Quebec. If you require an extra vote for that I am satisfied that the House would be willing to give an extra vote. We want to make a respectable showing at Quebec. I regret that you do not intend to mobilize the entire militia there as at first proposed. I believe that would have proved a splendid test of the strength of the military machine of this country. I think it is an unfortunate thing that the department has decided not to do it. I do not know the causes that have led up to that decision, and, perhaps I may be wrongfully finding fault. But, so far as it appears on the surface, I must say that this seems to be a bad decision. For, as I have said, this was an opportunity to test the machinery of the department. Now, it is a pretty expensive machinery, as the minister himself will admit, and the expense of it has been greatly increased within' the last few years. The only justification for that expense would be that it has given us a machine that will accomplish the purpose for which it was designed; and we have no way of judging whether the machine is a perfect machine as far as human machinery can be made perfect-or not, except by some such test as this. The mere fact of creating a certain bureau and giving the members of it high sounding names-generals, full colonels and so on-does not make that a perfect machine. The only way the government have of knowing whether this machine would do what it is designed for or not, would be by such a test as mobilizing the troops for Quebec. I regret very much that, for some reason, the department has seen fit to change its plans, and, instead of taking 30,000 or 40,000 troops to take only-is it 5,000 ?
Twelve thousand.
Well, that is not so bad. But still it seems to be a mistake for the minister to change his position.

I made a statement in the House as to the reasons for the decisions arrived at, and I do not wish to repeat it except to say that it was found to be absolutely impossible, with the means we have to mobilize 32,000 or 33,000 troops for Quebec at that time.
Why ?

Because the people who would require accommoda-tin on the trains going and coming could not be carried if we were to mobilize so many troops. More than that, the Battlefields Commission expressly limited us at the outset to a certain number of days- we must be through with our mobilization before a certain day, and we could not begin the returning of our troops to their homes until after a certain other day. This was all gone into very carefully, and it was found to be absolutely impossible to mobilize so many. We might have mobilized more than 12,000 but we could not do anything like 30,000 properly and with due regard to the comfort of the men. As to how we came to decide upon 12,000,1 would say to my hon. friend what I said in the House the other day, I think ; the Militia Department has received from the president -as I think he is called-of the Battlefields Commission a copy of a resolution passed unanimously by that body asking for 12,000 troops. It is upon that request that we are proceeding.; and I think' it is fair to assume that these gentlemen are the best judges as to the number of men likely to be comfortably accommodated both on the trains and in Quebec itself.
What is the proportion of rural and urban ?

I do not quite know yet, but to-morrow I think the general order will be issued. There will be something like equal numbers, probably rather more urban than rural. Now, as to the other point presented by my hon. friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), he may be perfectly certain that each rural battalion represented-and I hope they all will be ; they will all be offered a chance- will have the very best company that can be produced from the battalion. The hon. gentleman is familiar enough with the rural militia to know that a sense of pride will stimulate them to make the best choice, and the department, I can assure him, will co-operate with them in bringing about that desirable end.
Yes, but if you do not drill the regiment before the Tercentenary [DOT] how are you going to know ?
We have been drilling troops in this country for the last forty years, and the captains and colonels know where the men are, and, for an occasion like this, there will be no serious difficulty.
Is it the intention to select them individually from the whole of the regiment ?

My hon. friend knows that that is done every year. There is no permanency, no continuity, but every year the men who go into camp are selected about a week before. We are not going to prevent that now.
Does the minister mean, selected from the general mass of the population ?
Those that have been in camp for years.

But, for the purpose of sending a company to Quebec, are you going to take the whole of Company A, for instance, or are you going to select individuals from the different companies and make a composite company ?

That is a matter I am leaving in the hands of Brigadier General Otter, an old hand, who is arranging the details with the different colonels. We want to get the best results, and I do not propose to interfere. I have every confidence that Brigadier General Otter will do it in the best possible way, and I think we should give him the liberty necessary to bring about the best results.
But does not the minister think it about time the general community knew what line he proposes to take ? We are getting very close to the time when these people must go.
No doubt that is what will be done-it will be a composite company.
If it were known soon what is to be done, it might have some effect upon the men going into camp-it might be an extra inducement for men who have been well drilled to go into camp for that purpose.

Some companies were drilling expecting to be sent to Quebec- whatever the source of their information, that was their understanding. But since then, I understand, they have stopped drilling. It seems to me a matter of great importance that the men should know at as early a date as possible whether they are going or not. As to selection between the city and rural corps, I think there

ought to be a fair opportunity given to the rural corps to share in this celebration. Many of them have been disappointed because of the rumours in circulation lately that they are not to be taken. I know from letters that I have received that they are much disappointed, and very anxious to know how selection is to be made so that it may be known who are to go. It is getting very close to the time, and it seems to me that the Minister of Militia, with the council or whoever makes the arrangements, should reach a decision at the earliest possible moment.
It will be out to-morrow.
Would the minister tell us what officer of the general staff is in charge of the transport ?
Brigadier General Macdonald is in charge for the Quarter Master General, but Brigadier General Otter will have charge of the whole mobilization and will command this force at Quebec.

The point I want to get at is whether the Department of Militia and the Department of Railways, and the government generally, are satisfied with the capacity of our Canadian railways to mobilize a force of this size. I have been reading some of the statements made on behalf of the railways and it seems, they are rather disappointed. In fact, it does not seem to be so big a proposition as they make it out to be ; or, rather, it may show that their ability and capacity and equipment for handling a thing of this kind are not what they should be, and, from the national point of view, it might be worth some inquiring whether our railways are up to the mark of mobilizing our forces. To put the question in another way, any one attempting to invade this country would select a holiday, when the capacity of the railways was tested to the utmost, and there would be no means of moving o(ur troops. That is a very important question, and I hope the minister will give it some attention. He should see that the railways ol this country have an equipment enabling them to mobilize the troops under any conditions.

There is a great deal in what my hon. friend says. That is a very important point, and it has not escaped the consideration of the militia authorities. It is however only fair to the railways to say that if it were necessary to mobilize a considerable force at Quebec under stress of war or threatened trouble, there would not be much difficulty in doing so. But to undertake to bring to Quebec over 30,000 men, with a proper equipment of horses and artillery, while perhaps 100,000 people are to be brought into Quebec Mr. SPROULE.
and away from it at almost the same moment, is an entirely different proposition. It is something however that is not likely to happen. In time of trouble, under the Militia Act, pasesd a few years ago, the department can take possession of all the railways, and control them absolutely. In such a case the conditions would be entirely different from those which will prevail at the time of the tercentenary which is shortly to take place.
The minister said he had not decided as to the proportion of rural and urban militia that would be taken to Quebec.

Not quite that. I have not made up the figures. We have decided that one company of infantry from each rural battalion shall go to Quebec, or shall be offered the chance, and we have decided that half of the cavalry force shall go, and they are a rural force, and I think a certain amount of field artillery and garrison artillery. But the figures have not been made up yet.
What is the cost of transporting 12,000 men ?
I think the whole thing will cost, on the basis we have arranged, about $180,000; that includes food as well as transport.

The minister says he proposes to take one company from each rural battalion. Now there is considerable feeling in the country that the rural forces are not being fairly dealt with, that partiality is being shown to the urban forces. I do not say the department is doing that, but it is just as well that the point should be called to the minister's attention. I have a letter from the captain of a regiment calling my attention to this matter, and I will read it to let the minister know the opinion that prevails among some, at least, of the country militia. The letter is dated Bradford, May 25, 1908 :
As a member of the rural corps of the militia of Canada, I would like to see fair play handed out to all, as I think we have been unfairly dealt with in being denied the honour of going to Quebec.
We learn now that is not the case.
The city and permanent corps are only allowed to go, therefore calling out all of the rural corps that have played so important a part in the history of Canada. I need not tell you that the rural militia are the backbone of the country, and it will be a sad day if the rural corps are told to stand aside and make room for the city corps at Quebec.
The Minister of Militia need not tell the people that the railway companies are to blame in the matter, for as a matter of fact the transportation was arranged until the commanding officers of the city corps interviewed the government. We had orders to go

to Quebec fifty per cent strong some time ago, and soldier-like were making arrangements to go without complaint, not like the city corps for they began to howl. . . I am sorry to trouble you so, but as a member of the 36th regiment I want to see my men get fair play, and I am sure so do you, and in standing up for this regiment which is partly in your constituency, you will have the hearty support, not only of the young men who are in it now, but also of the parents and friends of numbers who have been members of the militia in their day.
Kindly take this matter up in the House, and I will await results.
I am, yours very truly,
GEORGE W. STODDART, Captain 36th Regiment.

Lennox,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
I therefore urge upon the minister to give the rural corps the fullest consideration. I may say, speaking of the militia generally, that there is a strong desire to go to Quebec. a very laudable desire ; so I hope the minister, if he errs at all, will err on the side of enlarging the force he proposed to send.

Having come into contact recently with military men, I have to say that there is considerable anxiety among them as to where they stand to-day. They seem to be entirely at a loss to know whether they are going into camp at all, not to speak of going to Quebec. I think the sooner the minister makes a definite announcement on this point the better, so as to settle the matter in the minds of the officers and men throughout the country. X know they are waiting anxiously, and there is a great deal of uncertainty as to what they are going to be called on to do. There is another point on which the men are uncertain. At present everybody is looking for some consideration for their time, and there is a feeling that it will be difficult to get men to go to camp unless reasonable compensation is paid. I do not know what the intention of the minister is, but I think he should not treat the men unfairly in this regard. I think fair compensation should be given them for the time they will spend in the military camps. I trust the minister will make a declaration to-night that may go broadcast to the country, and let every captain of a company know where he is when he asks men to join his company.

The minister is aware that I have urged upon him, publicly and privately, that as many of the rural corps as possible should go to camp. I was not in when he opened his remarks, and did not hear his reason for not taking to Quebec the rural corps to as full an extent as the city corps. I wish to recall the review before the Duke of York in the city of Toronto. The crack regiments of Toronto, Hamilton and almost every other city in Ontario were there. The minister
himself will admit that they took second place to several of the rural corps and one rural corps especially with respect to marching. drill, neatness or in every other way that any one could compare them. There were at least three rural corps from the province of Ontario that surpassed the city corps in everything except the fit of the uniforms and I am free to say that the 43rd Regiment of Ottawa was, in the universal opinion, the best drilled regiment and, like all other city corps they were neatly dressed, but in so far as military movements were concern ed the rural corps held their own -with the best of them, and some of the rural corps surpassed the city regiments. I would like to know why the rural corps should not be recognized in connection with this Quebec review. Why should not the minister adopt the old plan and take a half regiment from each locality to the city of Quebec ? X will give him fair warning that he will not have any military camps of the rural corps if they do not go to Quebec. I do not blame them. The men will not turn out to spend a few days in camp and see their comrades, with no greater claim to recognition, taken to Quebec. I am satisfied that the country would endorse the minister and that the transport could easily be arranged. Eollowr out the original plan, place 27,000 or 30,000 of the boys on the Plains of Abraham in July and the transport can be arranged. The transport can be arranged and I am satisfied that the House and the country will readily stand the cost. All the men want is to have their transport and ration allowance. I am satisfied that they will not ask for drill pay as the city corps are.
No.

The city corps wall perform their annual drill in the fall and spring and get their pay for it in consideration of which they will go to Quebec. The rural corps w'ill perform their drill and will go to Quebec and all they ask for is their transport and ration allowance.
The city corps will do their drill without any consideration at all.
Pardon me. They will get their annual pay for doing their drill in fall and spring, and they will go to Quebec and get their transport and rations but they will also have their pay.
They are entitled to it.

Certainly, but the rural corps will go them one better, if they get their rations and transport they will go to Quebec. If the minister does not take them he will not have successful annual camps. Why make this invidious distinction as against the rural corps ? I am satisfied that the House and the

country will back the minister up in taking the rural corps down there. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), an ardent friend of the volunteer system, I am sure, will join hands with the Minister of Militia in seeking to have this corps represented at Quebec. The transport matter is easily arranged. I will undertake to pick out half a dozen young fellows in the province of Ontario who would lay down a plan in half a day. The troops could be mobilized there without interfering with the ordinary passenger traffic. The militia will find that the rural corps will go if he will consent to give them their transport and rations. The city corps have made a deal that they will go under similar conditions but they will get their annual pay. Why should the rural corps be discriminated against?

My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) speaks-about the pay. The rate paid will be the rate prescribed by law-. It cannot be anything else. I will do him the justice to say that on several occasions before the pay was increased he participated in the demand that was made for an increase. Subsequently provision was made for efficiency pay of fifty cents for each militiaman; so much for the first year for efficiency, and so much for the second year over and above the regular pay of fifty cents per day per man. We cannot go beyond that. If a man goes to Quebec who has had three camps he will get 'a dollar a day and I presume that should be satisfactory. As to the observations of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes), he must have forgotten that we are restricted to 12,000 men.
Why?
Because the commission desires us to send 12,000 and no more.
Is the commission superior to parliament? The commission is the creation of parliament.

I know, but we have not the means of transportation. We have from 27,000 to 30,000 rural militia so that we could not possibly take even half of them and we must give due consideration to the city militia. The problem is a difficult one.
Why should the city corps be singled out? They are no better drilled.
I suppose they are entitled to representation?
Yes, but not to full representation in view of the fact that the representation of the country corps is but one out of eight.

They will not get full representation. They will all be represented. The two regiments in the city of Quebec, of course, will be taken in full. In reference to the plan upon which we are proceeding I think I had better say a word. In the first place we want an effective demonstration, we want the best show, because that is all it is, that can possibly be made there and we want the best review that has ever taken place in Canada. This will be the largest military review that has ever taken place of purely Canadian troops in Canada. There will be two thousand more men there than at the review at Toronto in 1901 to which my hon. friend referred.	.
The minister saw that review in Toronto and 'he told me himself that three rural corps were equal to any, and that one was superior to some.

I am very fond of the rural corps. I have been a member of -a battalion for forty years. Secondly, the representative character of this force must be looked at. I want to see representatives from every military district and every corps in so far as it can possibly be done. Due regard must also be had to economy.	We have no right to waste
money unnecessarily and therefore we should take those troops in the city of Quebec which will not involve any cost to the country and which are available. We should take our cavalry and artillery from the nearest point to Quebec, and it is proposed to hold one of the cavalry camps close to Quebec so that the cavalry can be utilized in the city. It will be composed of the eastern townships cavalry. These are the considerations which have guided us in the plan we have made in the carrying out of this review. From the west there will be two hundred soldiers made up of a composite corps from the whole of the Northwest including British Columbia. We propose in addition to bring the Royal Jlilitary College Cadets to the number of sixty. There will be from 800 to 1,000 horses including cavalry and horse artillery. There will be 1.400 officers, non-commissioned officers and men (about one-half) of the permanent force. There will be in all about 10,000 of the active militia; sixty Royal Jlilitary College Cadets and two hundred men from the west.
Where are the Army and and Navy Veterans.
I am afraid my hon. friend will be disappointed.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Victoria (Jlr. Sam. Hughes) as to the effect of the latest idea of the department with regard to taking troops to the review at Quebec. I think better of the militiamen of this country than to believe they would cease to belong to the

force simply because they did not get a chance to go to Quebec. No doubt every man in the militia would like to go to Quebec, but if that be impossible I do not think Jones will leave the militia simply because Smith goes to Quebec and he cannot. That is not the spirit which animates the militia force in the county whence I come. My natural sympathies would be in favour of the rural corps because I come from a rural constituency, but at the same time it is only natural to suppose that the city corps would be better drilled because they drill more and if they are of equal intelligence with the men of the rural corps they should be better drilled. The minister first announced that he would send to Quebec 50 per cent of the whole militia and I regret he is not doing so.
So am I.

If it is going to be a grand sight to see 12,000 troops it would be infinitely grander to see 30,000 from the standpoint of the pageant alone, and it would test our military system in a way that taking 12,000 troops would not. It seems to me the excuse of the railway companies is a flimsy excuse and that they ought to be compelled to take these men to *Quebec. You could arrange to take them there a day or two before. I do not believe that the men want to be paid for the time they are going to Quebec. I believe they would be very glad to go if they got their transportation, and their rations and their accommodation. A great many people are going there and paying their way to go and the military would be able to see the pageant even though they take part in it.

I agree with the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) that there should be no discrimination between the rural corps and the city corps. I believe that the rural corps are just as well drilled as the city corps even though they do not get so much drill. When they go to camp they go to learn drill and to learn something of the art of war, and we know they make better soldiers as a rule than the men of the city corps. I do not think there has been any valid reason given by tne Minister of Militia why the rural battalions should not be well represented in Quebec and I hope he will reconsider his decision in that respect. How many of the rural corps will go to Quebec now ?
One company from each regiment.
Who will decide which company.
The colonel of the regiment.
The colonel of the regiment has his favourites and I think it would be a fairer way for the men to draw lots.

I wish to express my dissent from the view put forward by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) that we should send the whole militia to Quebec, and I dissent on the ground that the expense of such a course would be enormous. The hon. gentleman seems to have ignored that point altogether.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me?
You will have an opportunity to speak later.
Does the hon. gentleman refuse me the courtesy of correcting him when he is misrepresenting me?
I have no intention of misrepresenting the hon. gentleman.
I will answer you later on.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) stated more than once that he was in favour of taking 30,000 of the militia to Quebec which is practically the whole of the militia of Canada. I cannot sit here without protesting against such an extravagant expenditure of money which in my opinion would amount to more than half a million dollars, il wish to point out to the House and to the people who pay the taxes that the hon. gentleman from Albert (Mr. Fowler) is willing to spend half a million in this way. He lectures us on economy but he is willing to spend half a million dollars on a mere military display which will only last a few days.

The hon. gentleman from Guysborough with his usual inability to grasp the sense of a statement and his usual unfairness in presenting his own views, has misrepresented what I said. When the Minister of Militia first discussed this matter in the House he said it was the intention to take o^^r cent of the militia force to Quebec ail^P: was with that proposition I dealt this afternoon. We were discussing only 50 per cent of the militia, and I did not advocate taking the whole militia of Canada to Quebec.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me ?

No, I wont, just take your seat. I will treat the hon. member for Guysborough with exactly the same courtesy that he accords to me and to other members of the House. I did not make any such statement ; but the hon. gentleman desired to make a political point against me, and he stated that it would cost half a million to take these troops to Quebec and keep them there for two or

three days. The hon. gentleman is not able to figure very well, or he would not have made that statement. If these troops went to Quebec, they would have no annual drill, as the minister stated before, so that it would not add one cent to the cost. My friend of limited understanding from Guysborough expresses very much solicitude and regret at this particular item on behalf of the dear taxpayer; but he sits there calmly and votes millions to be wasted in little twopenny-half-penny public works that are only temporary, that go out almost with the next tide, in the province of Nova Scotia. He is willing to vote hundreds of thousands to pay his illustrious friends of the North Atlantic Trading Company for bringing in many cases improper immigrants to this country ; and yet he holds up his hands in holy horror because a few dollars are to be spent to enable the rural militia to take part in this great demonstration that is to take place at Quebec. This is the hon. gentleman's idea of economy. If the electors of Guysborough were within the sound of the hon. gentleman's voice when he was giving utterances to these noble, patriotic and inspiring sentiments, I think his vote would be a very small one at the next election ; but I venture to say that the hon. gentleman does not talk in that manner when he goes into the county of Guysborough. When his friend Mr. Benjamin Franklin Pearson divided with his friends a little nestegg of $28,000 for which this country received nothing at all, the hon. member for Guysborough swallowed it as a baby would new milk ; and yet day after day. nisrht after night-because he is very regular in his attendance in the sessions of this House-he has sat in his place and voted for the expenditure of these huge sums for purchases which certainly do not inure to the benefit of the people of this country as a whole, but only to the benefit of a few favourite individuals.
Talk it out.

Hjei hon. member for Hamilton says, talk It out; but if the hon. member had put a muzzle on the hon. member for Guysborough, so much time perhaps would not have been taken up, and the item would have been through before. I am surprised that the Minister of Finance does not keep a better check on these irresponsible members than he does. Now I think this item had better pass.
I desire to ask the minister what proportion of the city corps and the rural corps is to go ?

I have not the figures, but I think there is something like an equal balance. There will be certain city regiments, and for the balance of the city regiments one company from each and one company from each rural corps.

Would the minister tell us what Toronto regiments are to
go ?

I could not say positively. I have an idea, but I think it undesirable to make the announcement at present. It will all be out in a day or two. I think two of the Toronto regiments are going-the Queen's Own and the 4Sth.
Why not the others ?
Perhaps they are but these have been mentioned to me.

I again want to impress on the minister that there should be a fair division as between the city corps and the rural corps. Unless the matter is arranged on an absolutely fair and square basis, he will find that there will be very great dissatisfaction on the part of the men who are left out, especially those of the rural corps.
I suppose the discussion can go on to-morrow on this same item if we carry it now ?

The same discussion can go on upon another item.
